snippet.title: Fallout Behind the Scenes - Turning Junkyards into the Wasteland

Fallout didn’t rely on CGI to build its world—because the wasteland had to feel real. Here’s how the team blended practical builds and VFX to redefine video game adaptations.

Fallout Power Armor: The Real Reason Season 1 Looks So Real comes down to something surprisingly old school: practical craftsmanship. In this behind-the-scenes breakdown, we explore how showrunner Jonathan Nolan and production designer Howard Cummings grounded Fallout’s iconic world in tangible details, from the Brotherhood of Steel suits to the grime smeared across Ella Purnell’s face.

The video digs into how the crew worked with high-end effects studios to create functional power armor—hero suits for close-ups, stunt versions for action, and destructible dummies for big moments. Instead of leaning on CGI junk, the team scavenged real junkyards, flea markets, and estate sales to build props that felt pulled straight from a post-nuclear America. This “found object realism” became a core long-tail approach to keeping Fallout’s aesthetic grounded.

We also look at the hybrid makeup/VFX pipeline that brought Walton Goggins’ Ghoul to life, why Ella Purnell’s daily makeup routine was so physically demanding, and how the designers balanced game-accurate vault interiors with the show’s need for texture and wear. From LED volume environments to 35mm film grain, Fallout Season 1 blends practical and digital techniques in a way that sets a new bar for adaptations.

With Season 2 heading to the Mojave Wasteland and New Vegas, these behind-the-scenes methods are only getting bigger.

snippet.title: Landman Season 2 Behind the Scenes
snippet.description:
Everything you see in Landman Season 2—every stunt, every negotiation, every moment of grit—comes from the real world. Here’s how the cast and crew built a show that refuses to fake the hard parts.

Landman Season 2: Theories That Explain Its Unmatched Realism digs into how Taylor Sheridan and his team craft a drama rooted in real oil-industry pressure, politics, and danger. From day one, the production commits to physical authenticity, pulling in roughneck veterans to train the cast on actual rig movement, hazard awareness, and the subtle physicality of workers who spend decades in the Permian Basin.

Billy Bob Thornton, Demi Moore, and Sam Elliott all credit this prep for shaping how their characters walk, negotiate, and react. Stunt sequences—pipe swings, ladder climbs, slips, and heavy tool work—are rehearsed on practice rigs before transitioning to full-scale builds, each one engineered for safety in unpredictable Texas conditions.

Shooting on location across Midland, Odessa, and surrounding ranchlands doesn’t just look good—it affects everything. The heat changes posture. Dust changes breathing. Sudden storms change pacing. The result is a world that feels lived in, not replicated.

Production design amplifies that contrast, rendering roughneck spaces as cluttered, muddy, and functional while billionaire offices remain sterile and controlled. It’s a visual language that mirrors the show’s themes.

What sets Landman apart is its journalistic backbone. Season 2 pulls heavily from real reporting—including insights from the Boomtown podcast—to shape storylines about mineral rights, old-money legacies, and moral gray zones. The actors use that research to fuel nuance and tension, making every negotiation and conflict feel earned.

This is how Landman becomes more than a drama—it becomes a reflection of the real oilfield experience.
